title: Humble before truth
hook: the dialogue ends with the yogis honoring the Word

segments.voice: Yesterday, the true yogi: spotless in the middle of the soot. Your line was yoga in daily life. Which ordinary thing did you do well? Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

An old-fashioned balance scale: two pans hanging from a beam. Put something on each side and watch. One pan rises. The other sinks. And the one that sinks is the one with more in it. Keep that scale in mind, because Guru Nanak used it. The Siddhs in the Sidh Gosht were people of standing, masters of hard disciplines, used to being the ones others came to. The dialogue is long, and the questions are sharp. So how does a meeting like that end, between people who don't bend easily? Today: humble before truth.
screen: `TWO PANS ON A BEAM.` → `THE HEAVIER ONE SINKS.` → `THE YOGIS BOWED.`

segments.voice: First, the ending. It's told in more than one place. The Sidh Gosht itself closes on the Word: in paraphrase, without the True Word there is no freedom, and the Gurmukh is the one who finds it. Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh poet whose Vaars are read alongside scripture, tells of Nanak meeting the Siddhs, and in his telling they end by praising the work of Nanak's life, a life spent pointing to the Name. Read together, the honor doesn't land on a debating score. It lands on the truth that was being talked about, and on a life that lived it. Now the scale. In the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak has a short verse about bowing. In paraphrase: everyone bows to themselves; no one bows to another. Put things on a balance and weigh them: the side that bows is the heavier one. That's a surprising way to measure a person. We usually think the one who stays upright is strong and the one who bends is weak. The verse turns it over. Bowing shows weight. The empty pan floats up. Right next to that verse, the Asa di Var gives two words that sum it up, mithat neevee: sweetness and humility, the essence of virtue and goodness. So when the yogis bow, this isn't a defeat on a scoreboard. Masters of their craft, they still had room to honor something true from outside their own order. That's heavy. And at the start of the dialogue, before a single argument, Nanak's first move was a bow to the True One. Humility runs both ways across that mountain.
screen: `THE HONOR GOES TO THE WORD.` · `THE SIDE THAT BOWS IS HEAVIER.` · `SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · `HUMILITY RUNS BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `THE YOGIS BOWED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone who taught you. This time, choose a harder teacher: someone who once told you something true that you didn't want to hear. A coach who corrected you, a friend who disagreed, maybe someone younger than you. Remember what they said, and how long it took before you could see it. Then, in whatever way feels right, lower your head a little. Not to make yourself small. Just to give the weight its due. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Humble before truth. The yogis honor the Word, not the winner; and in Guru Nanak's scale, the side that bows is the heavier one. Today's word.
Your line: the yogis bowed. Today, when someone says something true that you didn't think of first, say so out loud. Let your pan sink a little. Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib on entering a gurdwara, touching the forehead to the floor, and the Asa di Var, with its verse on sweetness and humility, is sung in gurdwaras in the early morning.

notes: The outline says the dialogue ends with the yogis honoring the Word. The script attributes the bow to the outline's reading and to Bhai Gurdas's telling, and summarizes the Sidh Gosht's close as 'without the True Word there is no freedom'. Please confirm both the paraphrase of the closing stanza and that Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, has the Siddhs praising Nanak at the end of their meeting (believed to be pauri 44, 'dhan Nanak teri vaddi kamaaee').

Asa di Var salok (Ang 470) paraphrased: everyone bows to self, none to another; weighed on a balance, the side that bows is heavier; and 'mithat neevee nanaka gun changiaaeeaa tat', sweetness and humility are the essence of virtues. Please confirm wording and Ang.
The Sidh Gosht's opening greeting of the assembly ('sant sabha jaikaro') is summarized as 'a greeting of honor to the gathering'. Please confirm.
howItsDone says Asa di Var is sung in gurdwaras in the early morning; please confirm or soften.

Editor: removed the spoken reference to 'the outline' from the hook; reconciled the teach with Bhai Gurdas (who has the Siddhs praise Nanak's life's work), so it no longer says the honor went 'not to a man'; corrected 'Nanak's first move was a greeting to the gathering' to his bow to the True One (day 1132 has the Siddhs greeting the gathering); reshaped the practice toward someone who told you a hard truth, since day 1141 already had 'thank a guide'.
